info.name: RealtorIQ — Broker API v1
info.description:
The JSON API the React broker app talks to.

**The flow chains itself.** Run the Auth folder top to bottom: `Request sign-in code` saves `request_id`, `Verify code` saves `access_token` and `refresh_token`, and every other request picks the token up from collection auth. Nothing needs copy-pasting.

**Prerequisites**

1. `bin/rails db:seed` — reference data
2. `bin/rails demo:seed` — a firm you can sign into (Sethi Realty)
3. `bin/dev` — the server on :3000

**Sign-in codes are `888888` in development.** Nothing is delivered. That is a development-only bypass; the app refuses to boot in production with it set.

**Error shape.** Every failure is `{ "error": { "code", "message", "details" } }`. Switch on `code`, never on the prose. The codes are: `not_registered`, `account_disabled`, `otp_locked`, `invalid_code`, `account_suspended`, `subscription_lapsed`, `device_limit_reached`, `forbidden_role`, `rate_limited`, `delivery_failed`, `unauthorized`, `not_found`, `invalid_request`.

item.name: Leads
item.description:
The core CRM object.

**Visibility is enforced server-side.** An agent sees only leads assigned to them; managers and the super admin see the firm's whole pipeline. A lead an agent may not see returns **404, not 403** — a 403 would confirm it exists.

**Two filter semantics worth knowing.** `status=missed_followup` is a *derived* tab, not a status: it means an overdue `next_action_at` on a non-terminal lead. And budget filtering is **overlap**, not containment — `budget_min`/`budget_max` return leads whose own range intersects your window.

Money is raw integer rupees throughout; the client formats lakh/crore.

request.description:
Default sort is a worklist: overdue followups first, then by when the next action is due.

Filters: `q`, `status`, `transaction_type`, `property_type_id`, `typology_ids[]`, `budget_min`, `budget_max`, `possession_from`, `possession_to`, `source_id`, `assigned_user_id`, `sort`, `page`, `per_page` (max 50).

Saves the first lead's id for the requests below.
The design's "Missed f/u" tab. Not a status — `LEAD_STATUSES` has no such entry — but an overdue next action on a lead that isn't already dead or booked.

**Name is optional** — brokers capture a number before anything else. Four fields are required: `mobile`, `transaction_type`, `budget`, and `property_type_id` *for sale leads only* — a rental lead carrying one is rejected, because the design's form never asks.

Mobiles are normalised to E.164, so `98201 44299` and `+919820144299` are the same number.

Duplicates are allowed (the design shows several leads on one number); the response carries `possible_duplicates` so the app can warn.

The pre-request script pulls a property type and typology id from /reference.

item.name: Uploads
item.description:
Direct upload: ask for a ticket, PUT the file straight to storage, then pass the returned `signed_id` when creating the record it belongs to.

Limits are enforced **when the ticket is issued**, per purpose — after that the browser talks to storage and this is the last point we control. Rails' own `/rails/active_storage/direct_uploads` is shadowed with a 404, since it sits outside this auth and enforces none of these rules.

request.description:
Purposes and caps: `booking_document` 2 MB (PDF/JPG/PNG), `project_brochure` 5 MB (PDF), `project_photo` and `property_photo` 5 MB (JPG/PNG/WebP), `firm_logo` 1 MB.

`checksum` is the base64 MD5 of the file — storage rejects the PUT if it doesn't match, which is the integrity check, not a bug.

item.name: Inventory
item.description:
Projects are developer stock a broker sells on commission. Properties are resale and rental listings. Buildings hold properties and are **firm-owned** — brokers create them inline from the property form, so one firm's typo never reaches another's dropdown.

**Inventory is firm-wide**, unlike leads: everyone in the firm sees all of it.

**Money is raw rupees.** The design's inputs read "₹ lakh" — that is a client-side unit, converted before it gets here.

**Price and area bands are derived**, not stored: min/max across a project's typologies. A stored band could disagree with its own rows.

item.name: Bookings and money
item.description:
Recording a sale and the brokerage on it.

**Managers and super admins only.** An agent gets `forbidden_role` on every request in this folder, including bookings for a lead of their own.

**Net income is computed server-side and stored:**

```
round(agreement_value × commission_percent / 100) + kicker − passback
```

The design's own example is the fixture: ₹1,56,00,000 at 4.5% is ₹7,02,000, plus a ₹50,000 kicker, minus a ₹66,000 passback = **₹6,86,000** — the "₹6.86 L" on its booking screen. The client never recomputes money; `revenue` carries every line already worked out.

**Two hard blocks.** Invoices cannot exceed net income; collections cannot exceed what was invoiced, and a payment naming an invoice cannot exceed that invoice. Refusals carry the arithmetic in `error.details` so the app can explain itself.

**Cancelling** sets the booking's status and nothing else — the lead is untouched and invoices already raised stay on record.

request.description:
Every booking carries a lead — the design's flow finds one by phone first, which is just `GET /leads?q=<digits>`; no separate endpoint.

`customer_name` and `customer_mobile` are **snapshotted** from the lead unless you send them: correcting the lead's name a year later must not rewrite what was booked.

The pre-request script picks a lead so the body doesn't hardcode an id.

exec: // Grab a lead to book against.
pm.test("net income matches the design's worked example", () => {

request.description:
Cancelled bookings are excluded unless you ask for them — the design says cancelling "removes this booking from revenue".

Filters: `q`, `client_phone`, `project_id`, `booked_from`, `booked_to`, `status`.

`totals` carries the firm's live agreement value and net income for the header.
The detail the design's tabs are built from: the itemised `revenue` block, documents, invoices and collections, plus `invoiced` / `collected` / `outstanding`.

The number is **entered by the broker**, not generated, so it matches the invoice they actually raised. Unique per firm.

Capped at net income — see the next request.

The number carries `{{$timestamp}}` because it is unique per firm. A fixed one 422s on the second run — and because each run creates a fresh booking, that left the next request with nothing invoiced and the over-invoicing check passed when it should have failed. Exactly the cascade running the collection is meant to catch.

exec: pm.test("the booking now shows it as invoiced", () => {

request.description: A firm cannot invoice more than it earned. The refusal carries `net_income`, `already_invoiced`, `attempted` and `available`, so the app can say how much is left rather than just refusing.

Modes: `neft_rtgs`, `upi`, `cheque`, `cash`.

`invoice_id` is optional — omit it for the design's "Unlinked payment". Attach proof by passing `proof_signed_id` from `POST /uploads` with purpose `collection_proof`.

Collected can never exceed invoiced. A payment naming a specific invoice is checked twice — against the booking's total and against that invoice's own amount, which is what catches a payment filed against the wrong invoice (`over_collected_for_invoice`).
Refused deliberately. A cancelled booking with no reason is one nobody can learn from.

item.name: Error states
item.description: The blocked states the React app has to render. Each returns a typed `error.code`; two more — `account_suspended` and `subscription_lapsed` — are produced by suspending the firm or lapsing its subscription in the admin panel, then calling `Who am I`.

request.description: Said plainly, because there is no self-signup: a stranger learning a number isn't registered gains nothing they can act on. The design's "This number isn't registered" wall.

Self-contained: the pre-request script asks for a fresh code first, so this works in a full collection run where `request_id` has already been consumed.

item.name: Sign out
item.description: Deliberately last. Signing out revokes the session, so anything after it would get 401 — which is exactly what an earlier draft of this collection did to itself.

request.description:
Always 204, whether or not that token was live — whether a token exists is not something an unauthenticated caller needs told.

Revokes the session, so the access token stops working on the very next request rather than when it expires.
